set1.q: Which change increases net fluid filtration out of a capillary?

Plasma colloid osmotic pressure pulls fluid INTO the capillary, so raising it reduces filtration.
A rise in interstitial fluid pressure
Interstitial fluid pressure opposes filtration; raising it pushes fluid back toward the capillary.
A rise in capillary hydrostatic pressure

Left ventricular failure raises left atrial pressure, but cor pulmonale is right ventricular DILATION driven by hypoxic pulmonary hypertension.
Embolism, dead space, hypercapnia, left atrial enlargement

Plaque rupture, coronary thrombosis, right ventricular infarction

Correct. Decreased plasma oncotic pressure, from severe hypoalbuminemia, nephrotic syndrome (protein loss) or cirrhosis (less albumin synthesis), lets fluid collect in the pleural space.
Decreased pleural space pressure follows lung collapse; nephrotic syndrome acts through oncotic pressure.
Inflamed, permeable pleura produces an exudate; nephrotic syndrome produces a transudate.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Obstructive pulmonary diseases
set2.q: What feature defines the obstructive pulmonary diseases?
opts: Decreased expansion defines the RESTRICTIVE lung diseases; obstruction raises airflow resistance.
Correct. Obstructive pulmonary diseases are manifested by increased airflow resistance, whether from the airway wall, loss of parenchyma or material in the lumen.
Interstitial thickening is diffuse interstitial lung disease, a restrictive disorder.
Air in the pleural space is pneumothorax, a pleural space disorder classed with the restrictive diseases.

set2.q: Approximately what is the normal mean pulmonary arterial pressure in a healthy adult?
opts: Eight mmHg is the normal pulmonary DIASTOLIC value (22/8 to 25/8 mmHg); the mean is about 15 mmHg.
Correct. Normal pulmonary arterial pressure is about 22/8 to 25/8 mmHg, with a mean of 15 mmHg.
Thirty mmHg is twice the normal mean and lies in the pulmonary hypertension range, not the healthy one.
Far above normal; the healthy mean is about 15 mmHg in this low-pressure system.

set2.q: What links each obstructive event to cardiac and cerebrovascular disturbance?
opts: Immune complex deposition is a type III mechanism, not the sleep apnea pathway.
No emboli arise; arousal-driven autonomic stress links obstruction to the heart and brain.
Ventilation repeatedly fails, causing asphyxia; arousals then connect it to autonomic stress.
Correct. With each obstruction, progressive asphyxia (lack of oxygen, excess carbon dioxide) and sudden autonomic and behavioral arousal result in acute cardiac and cerebrovascular disturbances.

set2.q: Which bronchiectasis shape combines saccular and cylindrical features?
opts: Saccular bronchiectasis is cavity-like dilatation, one of the two shapes fusiform combines.
Cylindrical bronchiectasis is the other of the two shapes fusiform combines.
Correct. Bronchiectasis is classified by bronchial shape: saccular (cavity-like), cylindrical, and fusiform (varicose), which combines saccular and cylindrical.
Centriacinar is an emphysema type that destroys respiratory bronchioles.

set2.q: What defines emphysema?
opts: Thickened, fibrotic alveolar walls describe interstitial lung disease, a restrictive disorder.
Reversible obstruction with airway inflammation is asthma; emphysema is irreversible alveolar destruction.
Permanent bronchial dilation is bronchiectasis; emphysema enlarges the distal air sacs instead.
Correct. Emphysema (type A chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, the “pink puffer”) is destruction of alveolar walls without fibrosis and abnormal enlargement of distal air sacs.

set2.q: Which finding confirms a restrictive pattern?
opts: A low forced vital capacity by itself does not establish restriction.
Correct. A low forced vital capacity alone does not establish restriction; a low total lung capacity confirms the restrictive pattern.
A low FEV1/FVC (forced expiratory volume in 1 second to forced vital capacity) ratio identifies obstruction.
A high residual volume supports incomplete emptying, an obstructive finding.

set2.q: For a patient already hospitalized for another reason, within what time of admission must respiratory symptoms begin for the pneumonia to count as community-acquired?
opts: Too short: patients hospitalized for under 48 hours before respiratory symptoms are still called community-acquired.
Too short: patients hospitalized under 48 hours before symptoms are still community-acquired.
Correct. Patients hospitalized for other reasons for under 48 hours before respiratory symptoms develop are also called community-acquired.
Too long: 4 hospital days defines EARLY hospital-acquired pneumonia; community-acquired is under 48 hours.

set2.q: Why does tension pneumothorax reduce cardiac output?
opts: The air stays in the pleural space; the problem is pressure pushing the mediastinum across.
The shifted mediastinum cuts venous return

Correct. Air enters but cannot escape on expiration and builds up under pressure; the ipsilateral lung collapses and the mediastinum is forced to the contralateral side, decreasing venous return and cardiac output.
The lung collapses, and air under pressure shifts the mediastinum.
Pleural air, not pericardial fluid, is the problem; mediastinal shift reduces venous return.

set2.q: Which category of acute respiratory failure shows hypoxemia with a normal or low carbon dioxide?
opts: Correct. Failure of respiration or oxygenation gives hypoxemia with normal or lower carbon dioxide: hypoxic respiratory failure.
Ventilatory failure is insufficient removal of carbon dioxide, so carbon dioxide rises (hypercapnia).
The combined category has both problems, so carbon dioxide would not stay normal or low.
Acute respiratory distress syndrome is one parenchymal CAUSE of failure, not one of the three categories.

set2.q: Which is a mechanism of HYPOXIC respiratory failure?
opts: Correct. Hypoxic respiratory failure arises from ventilation/perfusion mismatch, shunt, decreased diffusion, alveolar hypoventilation and high altitude.
Fever, infection and burns raise carbon dioxide production, a cause of hypercapnic ventilatory failure.
Inability to sense raised carbon dioxide
Failure to sense raised carbon dioxide, from drugs or alkalosis, causes hypercapnic ventilatory failure.
Failed signaling to the effectors (Guillain-Barré syndrome, spinal cord injury) causes hypercapnic ventilatory failure.

set2.q: What characterizes the end-stage (destruction) pattern of diffuse interstitial lung disease?
opts: Hyperinflated lungs with air trapped in the sacs
Air trapped behind airways that lost their radial traction is emphysema, which hyperinflates the lungs rather than stiffening them.
Dilated bronchi that act as pockets of infection
Destroyed, dilated bronchi that hold infection are bronchiectasis, an airway disease rather than end-stage interstitial scarring.
Lost alveolar walls and stiff, noncompliant lungs
Correct. The destruction stage is end-stage disease: alveolar walls are lost and the scarred lungs become stiff and noncompliant.
Inflammation is the early, reversible pattern; the end stage is irreversible loss of alveolar walls.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Asthma
set2.q: What mediates the immediate phase of allergic (extrinsic) asthma?
opts: Correct. The immediate phase is mediated by IgE to specific antigens; IgE binds mast cells, which release chemical mediators when the antigen arrives.
Sensitized T cells drive delayed (type IV) reactions, not the immediate phase.
Complement pores lyse cells; the immediate asthmatic phase is mast-cell mediator release.
Proteolytic enzymes from neutrophils and macrophages destroy alveoli in emphysema.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Obstructive pulmonary diseases
set2.q: What happens to the airways in acute bronchitis?
opts: Destruction of alveolar walls without fibrosis
Alveolar wall destruction without fibrosis is emphysema; acute bronchitis inflames the trachea and bronchi.
Persistent bronchial dilation from destroyed walls is bronchiectasis.
Bronchial gland hypertrophy over years of productive cough is chronic bronchitis.
Inflammation, more mucus, lost ciliary function
Correct. In acute bronchitis the airways are inflamed, narrow and swollen, with increased mucus, loss of ciliary function and loss of portions of the ciliated epithelium.

set2.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of pulmonary pathologies
set2.q: What does alpha-1 antitrypsin normally do in the lung?
opts: Correct. Alpha-1 antitrypsin is a protective enzyme that inhibits proteolytic breakdown of alveolar tissue; its hereditary deficiency causes about 1% of emphysema.
Surfactant is secreted by type II pneumocytes; alpha-1 antitrypsin is a protective antiprotease enzyme.
Proteases from neutrophils and macrophages DESTROY alveoli; alpha-1 antitrypsin opposes them.
Mucus clearance is the work of the ciliated epithelium (mucociliary clearance).

set2.q: What is the basic lesion of bronchiectasis?
opts: Alveolar destruction without fibrosis is emphysema; bronchiectasis destroys the bronchial walls.
Wall destruction that dilates the bronchi
Correct. In bronchiectasis destruction of the bronchial walls results in dilation of the bronchi: an obstructive, suppurative disorder.
Reversible spasm with airway inflammation is asthma; bronchiectasis is fixed wall destruction.
Gland and goblet cell hypertrophy with wall thickening is chronic bronchitis.

set2.q: Which disorder obstructs airflow through material within the airway lumen?
opts: Emphysema obstructs through loss of lung parenchyma around the airways.
Correct. Obstruction of the airway lumen includes bronchiectasis, bronchiolitis, cystic fibrosis, acute tracheobronchial obstruction, epiglottitis, croup and foreign body.
Asthma obstructs through conditions in the airway wall, not material filling the lumen.
Chronic bronchitis is a condition of the airway wall, not material filling the lumen.
